question: The problems within e-commerce have been known about for some time. At present, 20% of clothing bought online comes from China, 30-40% of which reportedly does not meet EU standards. Packages generally contain goods that are not so costly and therefore avoid stringent customs controls. Consequently, checks are carried out on only 0.005% of packages (1 in 20 000).

That means that many illegal products, such as smart vapes, are also entering the European market. Will the Commission work towards stricter rules on textiles labelling so that consumers can more easily identify products with a poor or a good social score and environmental score? On 31 October 2024, the Commission opened formal proceedings against Temu under the Digital Services Act.
On 5 February 2025, in addition, Commissioner Virkkunen will be presenting a communication on tackling challenges relating to e-commerce platforms. 1.

Many products from non-European platforms, such as Shein, reportedly do not comply with REACH, current environmental standards, rules on consumer protection and labelling standards. Does the Commission recognise these problems, and what will the Commission do to address them?
Hungary acts as a conduit for Chinese products that do not comply with European rules. What can the Commission do to close that conduit?
answer: The communication on a Comprehensive EU Toolbox for Safe and Sustainable E-commerce (1) proposes a series of measures to address challenges posed by e-commerce imports. In this regard, the Commission calls on the co-legislator to swiftly adopt the customs reform and to reinforce it with a handling fee on e-commerce parcels.

Moreover, the Commission has proposed a priority control area on e-commerce imports shipped directly to consumers with the cooperation of market surveillance authorities. An EU regulatory framework is in place to prevent the presence of hazardous substances in textiles, including imported ones.

Under the regulation on the Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of Chemicals (REACH) (2) several substances are banned or restricted and others may follow should it be warranted. The Commission supports Member States’ efforts in enforcing the regulation via the Forum for Exchange of Information on Enforcement (3).

Moreover, in line with the findings of its recent report (4), on the application of the Consumer Protection Cooperation (CPC) Regulation (5) the Commission is reflecting on a review of the regulation in order to further strengthen the enforcement of EU consumer law. The Commission is also envisaging a revision of the Textile Labelling Regulation and new eco-design requirements applicable to imported products.
